content: The World Health Organization (WHO) published its first comprehensive guidelines in April 2014 for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These guidelines aim to address the global burden of HCV, which affects over 185 million people worldwide, with approximately 350,000 deaths annually. Chronic HCV infection can lead to severe complications such as liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and many infected individuals remain unaware of their condition. Despite the availability of effective treatments, access to care remains limited in many regions. The guidelines are intended for policymakers, government officials, and healthcare providers, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, to support the development of programs for HCV screening, care, and treatment. They provide evidence-based recommendations to expand clinical services and improve patient outcomes. Unlike other chronic viral infections such as HIV, HCV can be cured with appropriate treatment. Advances in therapeutics have significantly improved cure rates, with newer antiviral medications achieving success rates exceeding 90%, even for previously difficult-to-treat genotypes. The document outlines recommendations for screening, diagnosis, and treatment, emphasizing the importance of early detection and intervention. For those with a positive serological test, nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA is recommended to confirm chronic infection and guide treatment decisions. Early RNA testing helps identify individuals who have spontaneously cleared the virus and those who require treatment. The guidelines also address the care of individuals with HCV infection, including the management of liver disease and associated comorbidities such as insulin resistance, diabetes, and lifestyle factors like alcohol use. Alcohol consumption can accelerate the progression of liver disease in HCV-infected individuals, and the WHO recommends brief alcohol intake assessments followed by behavioral interventions for those with moderate-to-high alcohol consumption. The WHO ASSIST (Alcohol, Smoking, and Substance Involvement Screening Test) framework is suggested as a standardized tool for alcohol screening and counseling. Treatment recommendations include the use of pegylated interferon and ribavirin as the standard of care, with additional options such as direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) like sofosbuvir and simeprevir for specific HCV genotypes. These newer therapies offer higher cure rates and shorter treatment durations compared to older regimens. The guidelines also highlight the importance of assessing liver fibrosis and cirrhosis using non-invasive tests like the aminotransferase/platelet ratio index (APRI) or FIB-4, particularly in resource-limited settings. The WHO emphasizes the need for integrated care, including vaccination against hepatitis A and B to prevent co-infections that can worsen liver disease. For people who inject drugs, harm reduction strategies such as access to sterile injection equipment and safe blood transfusions are critical to reducing HCV transmission. The development of these guidelines followed a rigorous process, including systematic reviews of evidence, expert consultations, and adherence to the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. The recommendations aim to provide a framework for expanding HCV care and treatment services globally, with periodic updates as new therapies and evidence become available.
